title: Seahawks Injury Update: Sam Darnold Cleared to Play, Star Defender Out – Field Gulls Report
body:
Seattle’s offense will get a boost on Sunday as quarterback Sam Darnold is cleared to play against the Washington Commanders, but the Seahawks’ secondary will be severely depleted with both starting safeties sidelined by injuries. Head coach Pete Carroll will have to adjust his defensive game plan while hoping Darnold can finally deliver the consistency the franchise has been chasing since acquiring him in the offseason.

The confirmation came from defensive coordinator Mike Macdonald on Friday, who said the former New York Jets and Carolina Panthers signal‑caller has passed his final physical and will suit up for the first time this season. Darnold, who entered Seattle on a three‑year, $90 million contract, has been under intense scrutiny after a rocky start to his tenure that included three interceptions and a fumble in his lone preseason appearance. The coaching staff hopes that a full week of practice will give him the rhythm needed to manage a potent Seattle attack featuring running back Kenneth Walker III and a trio of emerging receivers.

While the quarterback slot looks more promising, Seattle’s defensive backfield is in crisis. Starting safeties Jordan Pitts and Quandre Diggs, both key contributors to the team’s secondary, were listed as questionable earlier in the week. Further examinations revealed that Pitts suffered a high‑ankle sprain that will keep him out for at least two weeks, while Diggs sustained a hamstring strain that is expected to sideline him for the remainder of the season. Their absence removes the Seahawks’ most experienced tacklers and play‑callers, leaving rookie safety Jalen Campbell and veteran free‑agent signing Jamel Dean to shoulder a significantly larger workload.

The loss of Pitts and Diggs forces Carroll to lean heavily on his nickel and dime packages, likely increasing the reliance on linebackers Jordan Pacheco and Uchenna Ike Ezeh to fill the coverage gaps. Opposing offenses, particularly Washington’s balanced attack led by quarterback Sam Rivers, could exploit the weakened secondary with deeper routes and quick passes to the flats. Analysts note that the Commanders have been successful this season when facing teams with sub‑par safety play, ranking in the top ten for yards per pass attempt against secondaries that rank below the league median.

Seattle’s defensive coordinator Macdonald emphasized that the unit will focus on “gap discipline and aggressive front‑seven play” to compensate for the missing safeties. The Seahawks may also look to generate more turnovers through blitzes, hoping to offset the potential increase in big plays allowed downfield. However, the strategy carries risk; over‑committing pass rushers without reliable deep coverage could leave the defense vulnerable to quick strikes, a scenario that has plagued Seattle in several recent games.

If Darnold can manage the offense efficiently and avoid costly turnovers, Seattle’s chances of staying competitive against Washington improve markedly. Yet the defensive shortcomings could prove decisive, especially in a matchup that is expected to be low‑scoring and tightly contested. The Seahawks will need to rely on their running game to control the clock and keep the ball out of the hands of a Commanders offense that thrives on sustained drives.

Looking ahead, the health of the safety corps will be a pivotal factor for Seattle’s playoff aspirations. Should Pitts return after a short rehab and Diggs recover sooner than projected, the secondary could regain its footing before the crucial stretch run. Until then, the Seahawks must adapt quickly, leveraging Darnold’s return while devising schemes that mask the vulnerabilities in the back end. The outcome of Sunday’s game will offer a clear indicator of how well the team can navigate these simultaneous challenges and whether Seattle can remain a contender in a fiercely competitive NFC West.
